Claim: Every family of nonempty finite sets that is pairwise intersecting has only finitely many inclusion-minimal finite transversals.

Wait — this is related to a known result. Actually there's a known claim: "Every pairwise intersecting family of finite sets has finitely many minimal transversals" — hmm, actually the well-known theorem is that a family of sets has finitely many minimal transversals iff... Actually, minimal transversals of hypergraphs: a hypergraph has finitely many minimal transversals iff it has no infinite "antichain"... Let me think.

There's a classical result: A hypergraph H has finitely many minimal transversals if and only if H contains no infinite subfamily ... hmm. Actually the relevant known result: if H is an infinite family, minimal transversals can be infinite in number. For pairwise intersecting families — is there some theorem? Let me think about the proposed counterexample.

Family: F_n = {x_1, ..., x_n, y_n}, n ≥ 1. All sets are finite, nonempty. Pairwise intersecting: F_m ∩ F_n contains x_1 for any m, n (since x_1 ∈ F_n for all n). Indeed F_n contains x_1 through x_n, so x_1 is in all of them. So the family is pairwise intersecting — actually it even has a common element x_1, a "star".

Transversal: a set T meeting every F_n. Since x_1 ∈ F_n for all n, {x_1} itself is a transversal! And {x_1} is a singleton, so it's inclusion-minimal (any nonempty set's only proper subset is empty, which fails to meet F_1). So the minimal transversals: {x_1} is a minimal transversal. But the proposed witness claims T_k = {y_1, ..., y_{k-1}, x_k} are minimal transversals. But T_k contains x_k; is x_1 ∈ T_k? T_1 = {x_1}: yes, T_1 = {x_1} (since y_1..y_0 is empty, x_1). T_2 = {y_1, x_2}. Does T_2 meet every F_n? F_n for n ≥ 2 contains x_2. F_1 = {x_1, y_1} contains y_1. So yes, T_2 meets all F_n. Is T_2 minimal? Remove y_1: {x_2} doesn't meet F_1 (F_1 = {x_1, y_1}), correct. Remove x_2: {y_1} doesn't meet F_2 = {x_1, x_2, y_2}. Correct. So T_2 is a minimal transversal. Similarly T_3 = {y_1, y_2, x_3}: meets F_1 via y_1, F_2 via y_2, F_n (n ≥ 3) via x_3. Minimal: remove y_i misses F_i (since F_i = {x_1,...,x_i, y_i}, and y_j for j < i: F_i contains y_i only among y's; wait F_i contains y_i only, and x's up to x_i. If we remove y_i from T_k, does the rest meet F_i? Rest = {y_1, ..., y_{k-1}} \ {y_i} ∪ {x_k}. F_i contains x_j for j ≤ i and y_i. x_k ∈ F_i iff k ≤ i. But i < k (since i ranges over 1..k-1), so k > i, so x_k ∉ F_i. y_j ∈ F_i only if j = i. So rest misses F_i. Correct. Remove x_k: rest = {y_1, ..., y_{k-1}}. F_k = {x_1, ..., x_k, y_k} contains y_j only if j = k; but k > k-1 so no y_j is in F_k. So misses F_k. Correct. So indeed T_k is an inclusion-minimal transversal for each k ≥ 1, and they're distinct. So there are infinitely many minimal transversals.

Wait but does the presence of {x_1} as a minimal transversal matter? The claim says the family has only finitely many inclusion-minimal transversals. The witness shows infinitely many distinct inclusion-minimal transversals T_k. That violates the claim. But wait — minimal transversals: is T_2 = {y_1, x_2} minimal even though {x_1} is a transversal? Minimality is about inclusion, not cardinality. T_2 doesn't contain {x_1}, so {x_1} being a transversal doesn't affect minimality of T_2. Inclusion-minimal means no proper subset is a transversal. T_2's proper subsets: {y_1}, {x_2}, ∅. {x_1} is not a subset of T_2. So yes, T_2 is inclusion-minimal. Good.

So the witness is a valid counterexample, provided all hypotheses hold: family of nonempty finite sets — yes, F_n finite (size n+1), nonempty. Pairwise intersecting — yes, all share x_1. Transversals are finite sets meeting every member — T_k is finite. Inclusion-minimal — verified. Infinitely many distinct minimal transversals — yes, T_k distinct (T_k has size k... T_1 = {x_1} size 1, T_2 size 2, etc.). So the claim is false.

The counterexample given here is essentially the standard example: F_n = {x_1,...,x_n, y_n}. Indeed this is the classic example showing that an intersecting family can have infinitely many minimal transversals. Wait, but hold on: in this family, is x_1 in every F_n? Yes. Then {x_1} is a transversal of size 1. And minimal transversals T_k = {y_1,...,y_{k-1}, x_k} exist too. Interesting: minimal transversals can be arbitrarily large even when a tiny transversal exists. Indeed inclusion-minimality is a local property.

So the counterexample is valid and the claim is false.

"inclusion-minimal finite transversals (finite sets meeting every member)" — T_k is a finite set meeting every member. Inclusion-minimal among transversals: no proper subset is a transversal. Verified.
